You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test `testBase64EmptyInputStream()` expects that encoding an empty byte array (`new byte[0]`) results in an empty byte array output. However, the current bug report states that encoding an empty byte array returns the characters CRLF instead of an empty array.

From the code of `Base64.encodeBase64(byte[], boolean, boolean)`, we see that if the input array is null or empty, it returns the input array directly (line 684: `return binaryData;`), meaning it should return an empty array when encoding an empty byte array. This appears correct at first glance.

The actual encoding logic involves creating a `Base64` instance and calling its `encode()` method. The `Base64.encode(byte[], int, int)` method shows that when it receives an input length of `-1` (EOF), it checks if the line length is greater than zero and then appends a line separator (likely CRLF) to the output buffer (lines 446-449). This means that even if there's no input, if `lineLength` is positive, it will write a CRLF line separator to the output buffer.

The `encodeBase64` method constructs the `Base64` object with line wrapping enabled or disabled depending on the `isChunked` flag. It calculates the required output buffer length considering chunking and line separators. If line wrapping is enabled (chunked), then the final output will include CRLF characters even if the input was empty.

Therefore, the discrepancy arises when encoding an empty input with chunking enabled (line wrapping), where the output is not empty but contains CRLF. The test calls `testByteByByte(emptyEncoded, emptyDecoded, 76, CRLF)`, so `isChunked` is likely true or chunk size is set, causing the Base64 encoder to add CRLF even for empty input.

Hence the root cause is that the Base64 encoder appends the CRLF line separator on EOF regardless of whether any data has been encoded, resulting in CRLF output from encoding an empty input when chunking is used. The fix should ensure that if no data is encoded, no trailing line separator is appended.

The recent unrelated bug reports do not contradict this diagnosis.

This matches the current bug report title: "Base64 bug with empty input (new byte[0])" and description that empty input returns CRLF rather than empty array.

Suggested area for fix is in `Base64.encode(byte[], int, int)` method where the EOF handling appends the line separator unconditionally if lineLength > 0. Also possibly in `encodeBase64(byte[], boolean, boolean)` to handle the empty input case specially when chunking is enabled.

In summary:
- Test expects empty output for empty input.
- Actual output has CRLF due to appending line separator on EOF.
- Encoder code appends CRLF even if no data encoded.
- Fix: suppress trailing line separator if no data was encoded.

This explains why the test fails and is consistent with the bug report and observed code behavior.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
